extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetry, drama, and literary criticism; creative writers studying poetic and dramatic form
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and criticising poetry and drama (esp. tragedy, epic, comedy), describing what distinguishes genres and what makes a good tragedy (plot, character, diction, thought, song, spectacle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of imitation (medium, objects, manner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic arts differ from one another in three respects—the medium, the objects, the manner or mode of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three axes (medium, objects, manner) are the fundamental dimensions for classifying poetic forms; use them to decide whether a work is epic, tragedy, comedy, dithyramb, etc. (Examples and elaboration follow in the text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation (rhythm, language, harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation in the arts is produced by rhythm, language, or 'harmony', either singly or in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: music of the flute and lyre uses harmony and rhythm; dancing uses rhythm alone; some arts employ all three means (rhythm, tune, metre) as in dithyrambic and nomic poetry and in parts of tragedy and comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (types of characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of imitation are men in action, represented either as better than in real life, worse, or as they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representing characters as noble, base, or true-to-life is a key creative choice that determines genre effects (e.g., Homer makes men better than they are; comedy portrays them worse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation (narration vs presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may imitate by narration—in which case he can either take another personality as narrator or speak in his own person—or present all his characters as living and moving before us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction (narrative vs dramatic presentation) affects immediacy, point-of-view, and how plot and character are conveyed; it is one of the three primary differences distinguishing poetic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and core criteria of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with rhythm, harmony, and song; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this multi-part definition when judging a tragedy: assess seriousness, completeness (a whole action), magnitude, use of poetic ornament, dramatic (not merely narrative) presentation, and whether the work produces pity and fear leading to catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy must have six parts: Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each part as a distinct evaluative axis: Plot = arrangement of incidents; Character = qualities ascribed to agents; Diction = metrical arrangement of words; Thought = reasoning and statements of general truth; Spectacle = scenic and visual elements; Song = musical portions. Some parts form the medium (song, diction), some the manner, and others the objects of imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (structure of incidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most important of all is the structure of the plot; the plot is the imitation of the action and is the arrangement of the incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot (unity, causality, beginning-middle-end) is decisive for tragic success. When evaluating or composing, prioritize causal coherence and the ordered sequence of events over other elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot elements: Character and Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Character and Thought are the natural causes from which actions spring; Thought is required wherever a statement is proved or a general truth enunciated; Character is that in virtue of which we ascribe qualities to the agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether characters' dispositions and the intellectual content (arguments, revelations, decisions) plausibly and compellingly drive the action. Weakness in these will undermine the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and limits of Time and Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy endeavours, as far as possible, to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun (unity/limit of time), whereas Epic action has no limits of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider temporal compression in tragedy: constraining the action in time increases dramatic intensity and unity; epic allows broader temporal scope but should compensate by other devices (narrative breadth, metre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude and completeness of action
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must be 'complete' (a whole) and of a certain magnitude—an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the plot constitutes a whole with a determinate beginning, middle, and end, and whether its scale (stakes, breadth) fits the tragic mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction vs Song vs Spectacle (media and their roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the mere metrical arrangement of the words; Song is the musical element; Spectacle (spectacular equipment) is part of tragedy because tragic imitation implies persons acting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating language, distinguish metrical diction (word-level craft) from musical/song sections and from visual spectacle. Each contributes differently to the audience's experience and may be weighted differently depending on the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction: elevation with perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: How Poetry combines elevation of language with perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for elevated language that remains clear; avoid obscure ornamentation that sacrifices understanding. The ideal poetic diction raises style without losing communicative clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth vs common reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Elucidation of the meaning of Poetic Truth, and its difference from common reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether poetic representation achieves a truthful effect (plausibility, internal truth) distinct from factual accuracy. The 'air of plausibility' and coherence of the invented world matter more than strict realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between Epic and Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of difference enumerated: (1) the length of the poem; (2) the metre; (3) the art of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction. Epic admits one kind of metre (hexameter) and is narrative in form; Tragedy is dramatic and mixes metre, song, and spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these concrete differences when selecting genre and judging efficacy: epic's narrative sweep and single metre vs tragedy's dramatic immediacy and mixed media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metre and measure selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The iambic measure is the most colloquial and appropriate for dialogue; epic uses hexameters; satyric/original forms used other metres (trochaic tetrameter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match metre to function: choose iambic for conversational dramatic speech, hexameter for epic narration, and be aware how metre influences tone and perceived naturalness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and limits of Comedy (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is an imitation of characters of a lower type—the ludicrous being merely a subdivision of the ugly; it consists in some defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or judging comedy, distinguish the ludicrous from the painful; comedy targets defects that provoke amusement rather than harm. Consider historical development (late formalization) when comparing to tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic performance elements: actors, chorus, masks, scene-painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacular equipment (chorus, actors, masks, scene-painting) is integral to tragedy; historically Aeschylus introduced a second actor, Sophocles raised actors to three and added scene-painting; masks and prologues evolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider staging components as essential elements that shape the work's form and reception. Changes in actor-number, chorus role, and scenic practice materially affect dramatic possibilities and should inform composition and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation and human instinct: pleasure in likeness and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is an instinct implanted in man from childhood, and there is a universal pleasure in things imitated; the pleasure often depends on execution (colouring, fidelity) rather than on the imitation alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to exploit the audience's natural delight in imitation by skilful execution: fidelity of detail, apt 'colouring', and craftsmanship heighten the pleasurable effect even when the object imitated is unpleasant.
